name: Adaptation of Agentic AI: A Survey of Post-Training, Memory, and Skills
authors: Pengcheng Jiang, Jiacheng Lin, Zhiyi Shi, et al. (34 authors; Jiawei Han group). Lead affiliation UIUC, with Stanford, Princeton, Harvard, UC Berkeley, Caltech, UW, UCSD, Georgia Tech, Northwestern, TAMU, MGH.
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.AI; cs.CL). arXiv:2512.16301, submitted 18 Dec 2025, last revised 9 Mar 2026 (v3). Not yet peer-reviewed.
reflection_object: As a survey, it is an analysis (no single mechanism). It taxonomizes what the surveyed methods reflect on / modify: model weights (A1/A2 post-training), action trajectories and reusable skills/workflows (skill libraries), prompt/context and episodic memory (adaptive memory systems including episodic buffers, reflective databases, structured knowledge graphs), and the agent-tool interaction. The survey itself reflects on the design space of agent adaptation rather than performing reflection on outputs.
distillation_target: Survey-level: it catalogs all distillation targets used by surveyed methods — model-weights (post-training via SFT/DPO/RLVR), episodic-memory (episodic buffers, reflective databases), reusable-skill/workflow (skill libraries such as Voyager, EXPEL, JARVIS-1, CREATOR, ASI), and structured-rules/notes (knowledge graphs, curated reasoning strategies as in ReasoningBank). The survey treats long-term memory as a special case of T2 (agent-supervised tool adaptation).
emergent_vs_engineered: Discusses both: A2 end-to-end RL produces RL-emergent behaviors (self-correction, adaptive search depth, query refinement never explicitly supervised, e.g., DeepSeek-R1 'aha'-style emergence), while memory/skill systems and scaffolds are prompt/engineered. The survey explicitly contrasts RL-emergent strategic behavior (A2) against engineered modular tool/memory adaptation (T1/T2).
memory_type: Survey covering multiple: long-term-episodic (episodic buffers), structured-notes/graph (reflective databases, structured knowledge graphs), skill-library (executable-code skills, abstract heuristics, API/MCP protocols, synthesized tools, full-trajectory stores), and playbook/cheatsheet (curated reasoning strategies, e.g., ReasoningBank). Memory is framed as a special case of T2 agent-supervised tool adaptation.
memory_persistence: cross-session (production). The survey emphasizes persistent memory and reusable skills accumulated across episodes, tasks, and sessions (motivated by systems like OpenClaw that accumulate persistent memory and reusable skills); covers within-episode through cross-session.
memory_curation_mechanism: Surveys multiple curation strategies: self-summarized/curated (memory curators store concise transferable snippets — reusable strategies, code snippets, problem-solving insights — rather than full transcripts; ReasoningBank distills generalizable strategies from both successful and self-judged failed experiences, extracting preventative lessons from failures), retrieval-gated (RAG-style retrieval of memory/skills to guide future tasks), and overwrite/evolution (skill refinement across sessions). Append-only raw-trajectory storage is contrasted as the less effective baseline.
error_localization_granularity: Survey-level: the central A1-vs-A2 axis IS an error-localization axis. A1 (tool-execution-signaled) gives step-level/per-action dense feedback (e.g., code execution pass/fail, retrieval recall); A2 (agent-output-signaled) gives holistic/outcome-level sparse feedback on the final output with difficult credit assignment. Multi-agent/agent-level localization also discussed (lightweight subagents).
intra_task_vs_inter_task: Primarily inter-task: the survey's framing of adaptation is improving an agent/tools across tasks and sessions (transfer of experience via memory, skills, and weight updates). Memory and skill systems explicitly transfer experience across tasks/sessions; post-training transfers learned skills inter-task.
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: Survey-level / mixed: covers methods spanning mid-trajectory recovery (RL-emergent self-correction within trajectories in A2) and avoidance/learning-for-next-time (memory of failures, e.g., ReasoningBank's preventative lessons from failed experiences applied to future tasks).
task_domains: code (software development), QA/reasoning, web-navigation, computer-use, tool-use, decision-making, and scientific domains including drug discovery; general agentic AI. Deep research is a highlighted application domain.
benchmarks: Maps benchmarks onto A1/A2/T1/T2 paradigms. Mentioned suites include SWE-Bench (software development), WebArena and Mind2Web/web-navigation, OSWorld (computer use), GAIA (deep research/tool-use), and medical/general QA benchmarks; scientific tool benchmarks (SciToolAgent). Verifiable-execution metrics (pass@k, recall) vs holistic-utility metrics (final-answer correctness).
headline_result: No single model result (survey). Representative synthesis: s3 (a T2 search subagent) reaches 58.9% average generation accuracy using only 2.4k training samples — 70x less data than Search-R1 (an A2 agent needing ~170k examples) and 33x faster wall-clock training — and generalizes better (76.6% vs 71.8% on medical QA). Illustrates that T2 tool adaptation can match A2 with orders of magnitude less data.
baselines: As a survey it contrasts the four adaptation paradigms (A1, A2, T1, T2) against each other and against prompting-only / monolithic retraining; representative head-to-heads include T2 (s3) vs A2 (Search-R1). Also positions itself against prior AI-agent surveys as the first survey centered specifically on adaptation.
gains_vs_baseline: Survey-reported deltas for cited systems: s3 (T2) achieves 70x data efficiency and 33x faster training vs Search-R1 (A2) at comparable/better accuracy (58.9% avg; 76.6% vs 71.8% medical QA); SciToolAgent's knowledge-graph tool retrieval reaches 94% tool-selection accuracy, a 15-20% improvement over GPT-4o without tools. Core thesis: T2/T1 modular tool adaptation can match A1/A2 weight-update gains at far lower cost while avoiding catastrophic forgetting.
compute_cost_profile: A central comparative axis. A1/A2 (agent weight updates) are expensive (RL rollouts, gradient steps, GPU training) and risk catastrophic forgetting — likened to 'going back to college'. T1/T2 (tool/memory adaptation, frozen agent) are cheaper, faster, modular, and hot-swappable. Quantified: T2 method s3 uses 2.4k samples (70x less than A2's 170k) and trains 33x faster; T2 attains data efficiency by learning only procedural skill, not domain knowledge + reasoning + tool-use jointly.
known_limitations: As a survey it documents field-wide limitations and open problems: catastrophic forgetting in continual/open-ended adaptation; reward hacking / specification gaming (paradigm-dependent); unsafe exploration during on-policy RL in real environments; safety-guardrail erosion under aggressive RL (DeepSeek-R1 reasoning around refusals); difficult credit assignment under sparse A2 rewards; non-stationary agent-tool co-adaptation dynamics; and evaluation gaps (static single-score benchmarks fail to measure adaptation dynamics, stability, and safety trajectories). Survey-specific limits: rapidly moving field, no new experiments of its own.
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: Survey-level: explicitly organizes methods by feedback dependency. A1/T1 rely on external-tool/verifier or verifiable execution rewards (compiler pass/fail, recall, formal proof); A2/T2 rely on holistic output signals (final-answer EM, LLM-as-judge) and are characterized as more susceptible to reward hacking because of greater degrees of freedom. The A1-vs-A2 supervision-signal axis is the paper's primary discriminator.
self_correction_efficacy: task-dependent. The survey concludes adaptation strategy should match the domain: A1 (execution-based) dominates software development (deterministic test suites); A2 + T2 dominate deep research and computer use (non-deterministic / no test suites); T1 + T2 dominate drug discovery (sparse delayed wet-lab feedback). No universal winner; effectiveness is paradigm- and domain-dependent.
calibration_effect: not-measured (survey). It discusses safety degradation under aggressive RL adaptation (reasoning around refusal mechanisms) and reward hacking, but does not present a dedicated calibration/'reasoning tax' measurement.
failure_attribution_capability: classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy). The survey taxonomizes adaptation failure modes — catastrophic forgetting, reward hacking/specification gaming (with paradigm-dependent susceptibility: A1 hard to game, A2 sparse-reward susceptible, T2 tool-level reward hacking), unsafe exploration, parasitic tool adaptation, and safety degradation — but does not provide an automated step/agent attribution method.
failure_mode_addressed: Catastrophic forgetting (continual adaptation), reward hacking / specification gaming (e.g., trivially passing self-generated tests, manipulating evaluation state), tool-level / parasitic reward hacking in T2, unsafe exploration during on-policy RL, and safety-guardrail erosion. Conceptually overlaps with MAST-style modes (e.g., reward-hacking ~ task-derailment/specification gaming) but the paper uses its own adaptation-centric failure taxonomy rather than MAST's 14 modes.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: n/a. The survey does not release a new dataset or benchmark; it proposes an evaluation framework (four lenses: benchmark landscape mapped to A1/A2/T1/T2, adaptation-signal metrics, adaptation dynamics, safety) but does not publish a new resource.
builds_on: Positions itself relative to and builds on prior AI-agent surveys (which it cites as refs [1,15,16,17,18]); synthesizes foundational adaptation lines: DeepSeek-R1 (RLVR / on-policy RL for reasoning and tool use), Search-R1 / ReSearch / DeepResearcher (A2 search agents), s3 / AgentFlow / DynamicRAG (T2 tool adaptation), HuggingGPT / ViperGPT / SciToolAgent (T1 tool integration), Voyager / EXPEL / JARVIS-1 / CREATOR / ASI (skill libraries), and Mem-alpha / ReasoningBank (adaptive memory). Frames OpenClaw-style persistent memory/skills as motivation.
citation_count: 13 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026; influentialCitationCount 0). Recent preprint, so count is low and rising.
reasoning_model_native: Partially: the survey explicitly covers reasoning models with built-in/RL-emergent reflection (DeepSeek-R1 self-correction, adaptive search depth as emergent A2 behavior) and how RLVR post-training induces such behavior, but it is a general adaptation survey not exclusively about o1/R1-style models.
on_policy_distillation_link: Strong relevance. The survey foregrounds on-policy RL with verifiable rewards (DeepSeek-R1) as a pillar of adaptation, and its T2 paradigm (agent-supervised tool adaptation, e.g., s3) is closely related to skill/procedure distillation from a frozen agent's outputs — distilling reusable procedural skills into lightweight tools/memory rather than into core weights, directly relevant to on-policy distillation / skill-optimization threads.
sample_efficiency: Survey emphasizes sample efficiency as a key trade-off axis: T2 (s3) reaches comparable accuracy with 2.4k samples vs A2 (Search-R1) ~170k (70x more data-efficient) and 33x faster training, because T2 learns only procedural skill on a frozen, knowledgeable generator.
